definition: In deep learning, the transformer is a family of artificial neural network architectures based on the multi-head attention mechanism, in which input data such as text, images, or audio, is converted to a sequence of numerical representations called tokens, and each token is converted into a vector via lookup from a word embedding table.
details: At each layer, each token is then contextualized within the scope of the context window with other (unmasked) tokens via a parallel multi-head attention mechanism, allowing the signal for key tokens to be amplified and less important tokens to be diminished. Because self-attention alone is permutation-invariant, transformers inject positional information, typically through positional encodings or learned positional embeddings, so token order can affect the output. Transformers have the advantage of having no recurrent units, therefore requiring less training time than earlier recurrent neural architectures (RNNs) such as long short-term memory (LSTM). Later variations have been widely adopted for training large language models (LLMs) on large (language) datasets. Modern transformer designs are commonly grouped into encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder variants, depending on whether they are optimized for representation learning, autoregressive generation, or conditional sequence-to-sequence tasks. explainer.lead: In deep learning, the transformer is a family of neural network architectures based on multi-head attention, converting text, images or audio into tokens whose vectors are contextualized across a context window. It matters because it removed recurrence, enabling more parallel training.

tiers.eli5: The model turns everything into a row of tokens, then lets each token look around at the others to decide what it means in context.
tiers.practitioner: Each token is embedded via lookup from a word embedding table and contextualized by parallel multi-head attention at each layer. The pitfall is that self-attention is permutation-invariant, so positional encodings or learned positional embeddings must be added for token order to affect output.
tiers.paperLevel: Tokens are vectors obtained by lookup from a word embedding table; each layer contextualizes each token with other unmasked tokens in the context window via parallel multi-head attention, amplifying key tokens and diminishing less important ones. Positional information is injected because self-attention alone is permutation-invariant. Computations parallelize across sequence positions more readily than in LSTMs.

explainer.example: A word's token vector is looked up from an embedding table, then contextualized with the other unmasked tokens in the context window so its signal can be amplified or diminished.
